events.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and blast radius. Using query_metrics and query_logs, determine: (1) exact onset time of order-service p99 degradation and ledger-db statement timeouts between 2026-05-05T00:00Z and 10:59Z; (2) whether latency rose gradually or stepped abruptly; (3) which other services show correlated latency/error changes in the same window (list any service whose p99/error rate rose, not just order-service and ledger-db); (4) the specific error signatures in order-service and ledger-db logs (timeout type, lock waits, connection pool exhaustion, etc.); (5) resource trends on ledger-db and order-service (CPU, IO, connections, locks) across the onset.

Enumerate everything that changed on 2026-05-05 across ALL services. Using get_deployments and get_config_changes, list all deploys and config changes from 2026-05-05T00:00Z to 10:59Z (include service name, exact timestamp, and what changed), explicitly including database/infrastructure config changes such as the reported ledger-db autovacuum modification. Also search_historical_incidents for past incidents involving ledger-db, autovacuum changes, or order-service latency to find precedents.

Map the dependency graph around order-service. Using get_service_dependencies, determine the full upstream/downstream chain: what order-service calls (including ledger-db and any other datastores or services), what else depends on ledger-db, and identify any shared components or single points of contention. Flag any service in that graph that also appears in the change list, to identify candidate propagation paths independent of order-service.

args.query: ledger-db autovacuum statement timeout order latency

events.statement: Exactly one config change was recorded across all services in 2026-05-05T00:00Z–10:59Z: ledger-db config cfg-2903 changed autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor from 0.2 to 0.1 (description: 'More aggressive autovacuum') at 2026-05-05T08:00:00Z by dba-team. This confirms the DBA autovacuum change described in the incident report and pins it at 08:00Z.

Exactly one code deployment was recorded across all services in 2026-05-05T00:00Z–10:59Z: portfolio-service v4.5.0 (dep-5905) deployed at 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z by k.shah, summary 'Add realised P&L breakdown to holdings API', with changes ['new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at','no migration included'], status 'live' and rolled_back_at null (NOT rolled back).

No deployment or config change exists for order-service anywhere in 2026-05-05T00:00–10:59Z, nor in the preceding window 2026-05-04T00:00Z–2026-05-05T00:00Z (both queries returned count 0 for all services). This corroborates the report's statement that order-service 'has not been released this week' — any cause in order-service code/config is not visible in this data.

ledger-db is a SHARED PostgreSQL instance: order-service depends on it via a 'db' edge (order-service -> ledger-db), and portfolio-service (deployed 08:56Z with a new trades query) also targets the same shared datastore per the dependency graph showing ledger-db as type 'postgres', owner 'platform', shared=true.

Precedent search returned HIST-110 (2026-01-15, match_score 5): 'Slow orders from ledger-db IOPS throttling', services [order-service, ledger-db], symptoms [order latency, statement timeouts, slow queries], root_cause 'Cloud volume burst credits exhausted; IOPS throttled'. The symptoms match the current incident almost exactly but the recorded cause is a different mechanism (infrastructure IOPS, not config/autovacuum).

Earlier precedent HIST-111 (2025-05-22): 'Reporting job full table scans slowed ledger-db', services [ledger-db, settlement-service], symptoms [slow queries, high db cpu], root_cause 'New report query without index did sequential scans', resolution 'Added index; query review gate'. This establishes a recurring pattern where a NEW QUERY (not a config change) degraded the shared ledger-db and slowed its callers — directly parallel to dep-5905's 'new query on trades ... no migration included'.

Both change queries are point-in-time snapshots with no 'previous successful deploy' history beyond 2026-05-04T00:00Z, so I cannot confirm when order-service was last changed (the report says 'this week' but the data window starts 05-04).

events.answer: On 2026-05-05 (00:00–10:59Z) exactly two changes were recorded across ALL services: (1) cfg-2903, ledger-db autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 → 0.1 at 08:00:00Z by dba-team, and (2) dep-5905, a portfolio-service v4.5.0 deploy at 08:56:00Z that added a new query on the trades table (no migration) — a query-pattern change against the same shared datastore as order-service. No order-service deploy or config change exists in the window or the preceding day, consistent with the report that order-service was not released this week. The closest precedent is HIST-110 (2026-01-15, match_score 5), which had identical symptoms (order latency + ledger-db statement timeouts) but a different root cause (IOPS throttling), so symptom overlap does not confirm the autovacuum change as cause.

In the coarse 8-minute view the order-service p99 rise first appears in the 08:52:00Z bucket (avg 831.55ms), but the 3-minute zoom shows 08:54:00Z was still normal (149.12ms) and the actual step is at 08:57:00Z -- so onset is between ~08:54Z and 08:57Z, not 08:52Z.

events.answer: order-service p99 degraded abruptly (not gradually) at ~08:55Z, stepping from a stable ~150ms baseline to ~5.3s within one ~3-minute bucket (08:54:00Z avg 149.12ms → 08:57:00Z avg 1968.67ms, max 5607.8ms, then ~5.2-5.4s sustained). The first ledger-db slow queries appear at 08:58:38Z (application_name=portfolio-service), and ledger-db CPU/connections/slow-queries ramp in the 08:45-09:00Z 15-min bucket, with CPU locked at ~96% and connections ~190-210 from 09:00Z. Errors are statement timeouts: order-service logs "canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)" (284 in window, first 09:00:42Z) and ledger-db logs "slow query ... Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)" from portfolio-service. Blast radius and portfolio-service latency could not be confirmed due to budget exhaustion.

events.statement: order-service directly depends on ledger-db (kind 'db'), pricing-engine (http), exchange-gateway (http) and kafka (queue-produce); api-gateway calls order-service (http). This is the full 2-hop neighbourhood: pricing-engine fans out to market-data-service (http) and redis-cache (cache); exchange-gateway calls exchange-api (external, has_telemetry=false).

ledger-db is a SHARED postgres datastore (owner 'platform', shared=true, has_telemetry=true) with FOUR upstream callers via 'db' edges: order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service. It is the single point of contention where four services meet.

portfolio-service is also a direct caller of ledger-db. The only two entries in the 2026-05-04T00:00Z–2026-05-05T10:59Z change window are exactly the two services that sit adjacent to order-service through shared ledger-db: dep-5905 on portfolio-service at 08:56:00Z and cfg-2903 on ledger-db at 08:00:00Z. No change touches payment-service, settlement-service, pricing-engine, exchange-gateway, kafka or redis-cache.

kafka is a second shared platform component (shared=true): order-service and payment-service produce to it, settlement-service and notification-service consume. order-service hence has two shared-component fan-in points (ledger-db and kafka); redis-cache is a third shared component consumed by both pricing-engine and market-data-service/portfolio-service.

Propagation path independent of order-service: portfolio-service -> ledger-db. portfolio-service's new trades query (dep-5905, 'new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at', no migration) writes load onto the SAME shared datastore that order-service reads via its 'db' edge; any contention portfolio-service adds to ledger-db is directly visible to order-service with no order-service change required. This is the candidate propagation path consistent with the report that order-service was not released.

Telemetry caveat for the graph: exchange-api (external, vendor) is the only node with has_telemetry=false, so any exchange-side contribution cannot be observed in this data; all other nodes (including ledger-db, kafka, redis-cache, pricing-engine, market-data-service) report has_telemetry=true. ledger-db and the other shared datastores do expose telemetry but not the same metric set as services.

events.description: get_service_dependencies returns topology only; it does not return per-edge call volume, latency contribution, or which caller dominates ledger-db load. So I cannot quantify how much of ledger-db contention comes from portfolio-service's new trades query vs order-service's own traffic vs the autovacuum change from the dependency graph alone.
No dependency tool result exposes kafka/redis-cache metric names or utilisation, so I could not verify whether the other shared components (kafka, redis-cache) also show contention at ~08:57Z.

events.answer: order-service calls ledger-db (db), pricing-engine and exchange-gateway (http), and produces to kafka; api-gateway calls order-service. ledger-db (postgres, shared=true, owner platform) is the single point of contention: it is also a downstream dependency of portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service. kafka and redis-cache are the other shared platform components. Two services in this graph appear in the change list: ledger-db (cfg-2903, autovacuum, 08:00Z) and portfolio-service (dep-5905, new trades query, 08:56Z) — both are direct neighbours of order-service sharing ledger-db, so propagation via ledger-db is the visible path independent of any order-service change (order-service has none).

tasks.objective: Map the dependency graph around order-service. Using get_service_dependencies, determine the full upstream/downstream chain: what order-service calls (including ledger-db and any other datastores or services), what else depends on ledger-db, and identify any shared components or single points of contention. Flag any service in that graph that also appears in the change list, to identify candidate propagation paths independent of order-service.
tasks.answer: order-service calls ledger-db (db), pricing-engine and exchange-gateway (http), and produces to kafka; api-gateway calls order-service. ledger-db (postgres, shared=true, owner platform) is the single point of contention: it is also a downstream dependency of portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service. kafka and redis-cache are the other shared platform components. Two services in this graph appear in the change list: ledger-db (cfg-2903, autovacuum, 08:00Z) and portfolio-service (dep-5905, new trades query, 08:56Z) — both are direct neighbours of order-service sharing ledger-db, so propagation via ledger-db is the visible path independent of any order-service change (order-service has none).
